title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Word order is the English one — subject, verb, object — so a plain statement comes out in the order you already think in.

A verb ending already names its subject, so a neutral statement carries no subject pronoun: soy = I am, quiero = I want. yo and tú are not wrong, they are marked — they come back to contrast or to disambiguate (Yo soy de India, ella es de México).
You give your name with me llamo — literally "I call myself". The little pronoun says whose name it is: me llamo · te llamas · se llama.
soy is ser, the "to be" of identity and origin: who you are and where you are from. The ending names the person — soy (I) · eres (you) · es (he, she, and the polite usted).
After ser a profession or a role stands bare: Soy estudiante, never Soy un estudiante. un comes back only when something describes the noun (Soy un buen estudiante).

Every noun has a gender and its article shows it: el (m) · la (f) · los (m pl) · las (f pl). Learn each noun with its article — the last letter is a hint, not a rule, since el día is masculine and la mano is feminine.

Liking runs on gustar, "to please": the thing liked is the SUBJECT, so the verb agrees with IT and never with you — Me gusta el café (one thing) · Me gustan los libros (more than one). me only says who is pleased, and it never changes.
Spanish keeps the article where English drops it: Me gusta el café is "I like coffee", not "I like the coffee". A whole class of thing takes el or la.

words.note: llamarse, "to call oneself". The little pronoun says whose name it is: me llamo (mine) · te llamas (yours) · se llama (his or hers). This, and not mi nombre es, is how a name is given.
Names carry over unchanged — swap in your own.

sentences.trap: Mi nombre es Rohan is the English sentence translated word for word. It is grammatical, and nobody introduces themselves that way.
sentences.sound: ll sounds like the y in "yes" through most of the Spanish-speaking world: me YAH-mo. Both vowels are short and clean.

variations.changed: swap the name — Me llamo itself never changes
me → se: the same verb, a different person
a full noun can be the subject — el estudiante, and se llama gives his name

mistake.why: No es — llamo is already the verb. Me llamo Rohan is the whole sentence.

sentences.mnemonic: llamo = I call. Your name is what you call yourself, so me llamo.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Am from India" — the "I" is inside soy

words.note: ser — the "to be" of identity and origin: who you are, and where you are from. The ending names the person: soy (I) · eres (you) · es (he, she, usted). M2 brings in the other "to be", estar.
One little word for both "from" and "of": soy de India (from), estudiante de español (of).
Country names mostly carry over, capital letter and all.

sentences.trap: English says the "I" out loud every time. Yo soy de India is not wrong, but it reads as insistence — I am from India, whatever you are. The neutral sentence is Soy de India.
sentences.sound: Soy rhymes with English "boy". India starts EEN-, never EYE-, and every vowel stays short.

variations.changed: swap the place — Soy de … is the frame
soy → es: the ending swaps the person, and still no pronoun
soy takes your name too — and the origin tags along after a comma

mistake.why: Drop the yo — soy already says "I am". It comes back only when you are drawing a contrast.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second or third line of any introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: ser is the verb of who and of where from: soy de … — I am of that place.

sentences.cue: I am a student of Spanish
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Am student of Spanish" — there is no word for "a"

words.note: One shape for a man and for a woman — el estudiante · la estudiante — so only the article moves. Plural estudiantes.
The language, and also the adjective. As an adjective it agrees with what it describes: español for a masculine noun, española for a feminine one — la música española. Languages take a small letter.

sentences.trap: English needs the article — I am a student — and Spanish refuses it after ser. Soy un estudiante only works once something describes the noun: Soy un buen estudiante.
sentences.sound: Spanish cannot begin a word with s plus a consonant, so "student" became estudiante and "school" is escuela. Say that opening e-. español ends on its stressed -ñol, and ñ is the ny of "canyon".

variations.changed: swap what you study — de is what links the two nouns
any profession fits the frame, and there is still no un

variations.cue: I am a student of Spanish music
variations.changed: the adjective agrees inside the de phrase — española follows música

mistake.why: Drop the un. After ser, a bare role is the everyday sentence: Soy estudiante de español.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do — work or study — when you meet someone.
sentences.mnemonic: Spanish states the role, not a count of it: Soy estudiante.

words.note: gustar means "to please", so the thing liked is the subject and gusta agrees with it: one thing → gusta. The pronoun in front says who is pleased: me gusta · te gusta · le gusta. Plural: me gustan.
The masculine singular article, and the article shows a noun's gender: el (m) · la (f) · los (m pl) · las (f pl). Spanish also keeps it where English drops it — me gusta el café is "I like coffee".
Masculine, so el café. Plural cafés, and the written accent stays where it was.

sentences.trap: Yo gusto el café copies the English shape and ends up saying that you are the one doing the pleasing.
sentences.sound: Stress lands on the last syllable — ka-FEH — which is exactly what the written accent is telling you.

variations.changed: me → te: who is pleased changes, gusta does not
swap the thing liked — still one thing, so still gusta
me → le: now she is the one pleased — gusta still does not move

mistake.why: gustar runs the other way: the coffee pleases you. Me gusta el café.

sentences.usage: Likes of every kind — food, music, places, people.
sentences.mnemonic: Read it backwards and it clicks: to-me pleases the coffee.

words.note: The feminine singular article. Gender belongs to the noun and not to its last letter: el día ends in -a and is masculine, la mano ends in -o and is feminine. Learn each noun with its article.
Feminine, so la música. The written accent throws the stress three syllables back: MÚ-si-ca.

sentences.trap: It is still one thing being liked, so it is still gusta — music does not go plural just because there is a lot of it.
sentences.sound: MÚ-si-ca. The u is the oo of "moon", cut short, and the accent marks the stressed syllable.

variations.changed: add an adjective and it agrees with música — española, not español
me → te: the person pleased changes, gusta stays
me → le: her liking now — the pronoun set is me · te · le, and gusta stays put

mistake.why: English says "I like music" with no "the"; Spanish needs the article for a whole class of thing: Me gusta la música.

sentences.usage: Talking about what you enjoy — usually the first thing anyone asks.
sentences.mnemonic: A whole class of thing carries its article: la música, el café.

words.note: The plural partner of S04's me gusta. More than one thing does the pleasing, so the verb goes plural — gustan. The things decide, never you: only the pronoun swaps — me gustan · te gustan · le gustan.
Masculine plural. The noun takes -s and the article goes plural with it: el libro → los libros.
Masculine: el libro (one) · los libros (more than one).

sentences.trap: English keeps "like" flat — I like a book, I like books. Spanish moves the verb, because the books are its subject.
sentences.sound: LI-bros, stressed on the first syllable, and the single r is one quick tap of the tongue — nothing like the English r.

variations.changed: one book, so gusta and el come back
me → te: the person pleased changes, gustan does not
me → le: a third person is pleased, and gustan still agrees with the books

mistake.why: Two or more things are doing the pleasing, so the verb is plural: Me gustan los libros.

sentences.usage: Saying what you like when there is more than one of it.
sentences.mnemonic: Count the things, not the people: one → gusta, many → gustan.

words.note: Feminine plural: la película → las películas. Four articles in all — el · la · los · las — one for each pairing of gender and number.
Feminine: la película (one) · las películas (more than one). It is the everyday word for a film or a movie.

sentences.trap: The article is doing work English does with nothing at all: "I like films" is me gustan LAS películas.
sentences.sound: pe-LÍ-cu-la. The accent is written because the stress falls back onto the third-from-last syllable.

variations.changed: one film: la, and gusta
mucho goes straight after the verb
me → te: the person pleased changes, and gustan stays with the films

mistake.why: película is feminine, so its plural article is las: las películas.

sentences.usage: Films, food, music — anything you like in the plural.
sentences.mnemonic: las películas — the article and the noun end in -as together.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "I-want coffee" — there is no word for "some"

words.note: querer — to want. The ending names the person: quiero (I) · quieres (you, which M3 teaches as a row of its own) · quiere (he or she, and usted). Aimed at a person it also means to love: te quiero.

sentences.trap: English needs "some coffee" or "a coffee"; Spanish is content with the bare noun — Quiero café.
sentences.sound: qu is simply a k: KYEH-ro. The u is silent, exactly as it is in queso.

variations.changed: swap what you want — Quiero + the thing
the ending changes the person, and there is still no pronoun
-o → -e: a third person wants, and there is still no pronoun

mistake.why: Drop the yo — quiero already means "I want". Keep it only to contrast with someone else.

sentences.usage: Asking for something plainly. Softer ways of asking come later; this one is direct, not rude.

words.note: Feminine — but in the singular it borrows el, because it begins with a stressed a-: el agua, never la agua. M3 comes back to it.

sentences.trap: Water is a mass noun in both languages, so no article is needed here. Add one in the singular, though, and it is el agua.
sentences.sound: AH-gwa. gu before an a is a hard g with a w-glide, one syllable — not AH-goo-a.

variations.changed: that particular water — and the article is el, not la
-o → -e: the ending names a different person
the other frame — liking runs on me gusta, and the article comes back with it

mistake.why: In the singular agua takes el — el agua. The noun is still feminine; the article is only dodging two stressed a's in a row.

sentences.usage: The most useful request in the language.
sentences.mnemonic: Two stressed a's collide in la agua, so Spanish says el agua.

words.note: a lot, and it sits right after the verb: me gusta mucho el español, never me gusta el español mucho. Before a noun it is an adjective and agrees (mucho café · mucha agua); as the adverb it is fixed.

sentences.trap: English hangs "a lot" on the end of the sentence. Spanish presses it against the verb.
sentences.sound: MU-cho. The ch is the ch of "church" and the final o is short.

variations.changed: plural things → gustan, and mucho stays put
swap the thing liked; the frame holds
the liked thing is the real subject, so it can stand in front — and mucho stays glued to gusta

mistake.why: mucho belongs right after the verb: Me gusta mucho el español.

sentences.usage: Turning a like up a notch without reaching for a new verb.

comprehensionPool.display: Me gusta la música de India
comprehensionPool.cue: I like the music of India
